text.p: Molybdenum prices continued to consolidate after the volatility of recent months, although small, cash-strapped Chinese producers were offering ferro-molybdenum at prices below world market levels, traders said on Tuesday.
In the cobalt market, Japanese traders said prices were holding steady to slightly firmer, although the direction was unclear for the near term.
One trader of minor metals in Hong Kong said some small Chinese ferro-molybdenum producers were selling cheaply in order to raise cash for year-end loan repayments.

"Nine dollars (a kg) is reasonable but the Chinese producers must sell lower because they can't keep the material and the banks must call in loans," he said, adding that he bought two 20-tonne containers at $8.50 a kg for sale to Europe.

A trader at a large Japanese trade house said, however, that ferro-molybdenum prices had mostly edged back above the $9.00 a kg level after their recent slide, while molybdenum oxide was back above $4.00 a lb.
He suspected the cheaper Chinese material was of low quality.

Song Xiaoying, managing director of Chinese trading house Shangxiang Minmetals Holding Ltd in Hong Kong, said the molybdenum market was consolidating after gains he described as "too much, too fast" in the third quarter of this year.
He added that Chinese producers would begin to lose money if they sold ferro-molybdenum below $9.50 a lb, "but they have to sell".
"When the market price goes up they hold, and even though they might have had a contract they want to re-negotiate (the price)," he said. "Then when the market falls they want to ship."

In the cobalt market, Japanese traders said the gap between Russian and high-grade metal had narrowed somewhat, with the former quoted at about $21 a lb and the latter at about $22, and this was keeping interest in Russian metal low.

One trader added that although there were conflicting forces in the market attempting to lift or depress prices, there had not been much change in underlying supply and demand factors since a modest firming in prices early this month.
He attributed the widely conflicting views of the market in part to traders attempting to influence prices going into next month's scheduled bidding for U.S. Defense Logistics Agency stockpile sales.
Another trader added that cobalt demand from Japan's battery sector, where surplus inventories appeared to have been worked off, was helping to support the market in Japan.
In the market for gallium, used in semiconductor production, Chinese demand remained steady.
One trader said the provincial branch of a major state-owned metals firm would complete its planned purchase of 10 tonnes before the year-end.
It purchased four tonnes of gallium in mid-1996 at $370 and $390 a kg, although the buying dried up after prices spiked above $400, he said.
"I think they will be interested in finishing their buying plans soon with prices how they are now," he said. Gallium ingot was indicated last week at $354 a kg.
"The price is good at the moment. General consumption and demand is quite good, especially in Japan," the trader said.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Hong Kong New Desk +85-2-2843-6470
-- Edmund Klamann, Tokyo Commodity Desk +81-3-3432-6179
